reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it promotes Forsage BUSD through claims of seven-figure weekly earnings, over $200,000 generated in 10 days, and at least $10,000 per month by copying the presenter. It directs viewers to obtain BNB and BUSD, pay to activate and register matrix slots, and provide personal and account information. The earning mechanism also involves recruitment, affiliate-link registration, and reusing the webinar to promote the project to others.

opening.argument: The presentation expressly addresses the obvious concern that a crypto project might be unsafe. The speaker says there is “no need to worry” about hackers or scams because the project is decentralized and its transactions are verifiable on the blockchain. That is a substantive explanation of the claimed safeguards, not concealment of how the system is presented. The speaker also describes transparency as a benefit and says transactions can be checked independently. A judge should therefore read the promotional language alongside its stated decentralization and verification rationale, rather than treating every optimistic statement as proof of deceptive intent.

citations.quote: Transparency is super transparent. All the transactions are verifiable on the binance smart chain blockchain
there's no need to worry about hackers or the projects scams
the project cannot scam for the same reason that the project creators they never ever keep the crypto off the members

rebuttal.rebuttal: The cited earnings and participation instructions do not establish that the speaker concealed risks. The presentation expressly discusses decentralization, blockchain verification, and why the speaker believes centralized theft or disappearance is less applicable. Those statements may be optimistic, but optimism is not itself proof that the project was presented deceptively.

citations.quote: all the transactions are happening on the blockchain that you can go and verify for sell
there is no centralized funds

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The assurances are conclusions, not independent evidence that participants will be protected or paid. Saying transactions are visible does not show that the underlying income model is sustainable, and saying creators do not hold members’ crypto does not eliminate the possibility of losses. The same presentation pairs those assurances with extraordinary income claims and recruitment-dependent cycling.

citations.quote: the project cannot scam for the same reason

opening.argument: The video is structured as a webinar and operational walkthrough. The speaker explains how the front end reflects activity on the blockchain, demonstrates account access, describes the X3 and X4 matrices, and walks through wallet and registration procedures. He repeatedly frames the material as teaching viewers how the system works and offers tutorials for setup. Showing dashboards, explaining slot mechanics, and demonstrating access are educational and operational features; they do not by themselves prove that every income example is a guarantee or that the presentation is a scam.

citations.quote: welcome everyone to this exciting webinar
This is what you see right now. This is the front end. This is the back office
we have tutorials on how to do it
x3 matrix is very simple matrix guys it has 12 slots

rebuttal.rebuttal: The existence of a webinar and demonstrations does not turn the content into a deceptive solicitation. The speaker explains the interfaces and matrix rules in concrete terms, including how slots and cycles are represented. The evidence supports an instructional presentation about operating the system, even if the presenter also uses promotional language.

citations.quote: we'll talk about the x3 and x4 matrixes and how do you work
you will see exactly what you need to do how to install it and follow step by step

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The instructional format is precisely what makes the promotion actionable. The walkthrough does not merely analyze a system: it tells viewers to obtain BNB and BUSD, activate slots, register, and use a promotional link. Calling those steps educational does not change that the stated lesson is how to participate and earn through the matrix.

opening.argument: The material can be understood as promotion of a blockchain-based service with optional referral features, not proof of a classic scam mechanism. The cited record does not show the presenter taking custody of viewers’ funds, requesting a completed payment in the video, or promising that every viewer will receive a particular return. The registration page displays ordinary account fields, while the system is described as using users’ own wallets and blockchain transactions. The reference-side quotations identify a matrix and referrals, but they do not independently establish that the service is fraudulent or that losses are inevitable.

citations.quote: the project creators they never ever keep the crypto off the members
BNB used for fees and BUSD for activating the slots
all the transactions are happening on the blockchain

rebuttal.rebuttal: The presence of affiliate links and account setup is also consistent with ordinary referral-based commerce. The cited passages do not show the speaker personally collecting deposits, possessing viewers’ passwords, or guaranteeing a fixed return. They describe how the service is accessed and how users can promote it, leaving the alleged scam mechanism unproven.

citations.quote: click the link below this video and register
you can take this very webinar right now

true_side_reply.rebuttal: This is not merely ordinary referral marketing: the described income depends on paid slots, placement in a matrix, cycling, and bringing in participants through affiliate links. The speaker explicitly describes payment when people land in positions and says a participant’s activity can keep generating income. The absence of a completed transaction on camera does not remove the mechanism being promoted.
